Maladaptive Strategies.value: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts
give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Negative Appraisals.value: I should have protected others and I failed
I am permanently an outsider now

vignette: Sara, a 68-year-old Middle Eastern woman and retired prison guard, has been experiencing significant distress since an assault she endured six months ago. The traumatic event involved being physically attacked by one of the inmates during her night shift, which left her feeling vulnerable and unsafe. This incident not only shattered her sense of security but also deepened her feelings of failure for not having protected herself and others. Sara had come to believe that she failed to protect those around her because she was overwhelmed by the situation. She felt an intense burden of guilt for not preventing the attack, which led her to adopt several maladaptive strategies as a coping mechanism. One such strategy is constantly socializing; Sara finds herself surrounded by people all the time, never allowing herself to be alone with her thoughts. This constant need for company stems from her deep-seated fear that being alone would leave her vulnerable and exposed. Her mistrust of others has grown since the assault, making it difficult for her to feel safe in any environment. Sara is constantly scanning her surroundings, looking for signs of potential danger. She believes that people cannot be trusted, which exacerbates her feelings of being an outsider. This sense of mistrust also fuels her belief that she should have done more to protect herself and others during the assault. The combination of these negative appraisals has led Sara to drop important responsibilities at home, such as cooking or cleaning, because she feels it keeps her safer by avoiding potential triggers. She is convinced that any moment alone could lead to another dangerous situation. This pattern of thought also leads her to experience severe sleep problems. Her body reacts before her mind can process what’s happening, leaving her hypervigilant and unable to relax. One evening, Sara was at home when an unusual silence enveloped the house. This silence triggered a wave of anxiety, making her feel as though something dangerous was about to happen. She immediately checked all doors and windows, ensuring they were locked and secure. Her body reacted before she could think logically, causing her heart rate to spike and her muscles to tense. These experiences have further reinforced Sara's negative appraisals that she is permanently an outsider and that people cannot be trusted. This cycle of fear and mistrust has made it increasingly difficult for her to maintain relationships and perform daily tasks without feeling overwhelmed by anxiety. Over the past few months, these maladaptive strategies have taken a toll on her marriage. Her husband feels alienated by her constant need for socialization and her dropping of responsibilities at home. He is concerned about Sara’s well-being but struggles to understand why she behaves this way. What finally brought Sara to seek help was a realization that her coping mechanisms were no longer working and were instead making her feel worse. She fears being alone, yet her constant socializing has left her feeling exhausted and disconnected from reality. The most hopeful part of seeking therapy is the possibility of finding new ways to manage her fear and rebuild trust in herself and others. Sara’s story highlights a complex interplay between negative appraisals, maladaptive strategies, and heightened threat perceptions that have created a self-reinforcing cycle of distress. Her experiences are grounded in her deep-seated fears and beliefs about safety and trust, which continue to impact every aspect of her life.
